text: My spirit is broken, my days are snuffed out, the graves are ready for me.

versions.text: My spirit is broken, my days are snuffed out, the grave is waiting for me.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew קְבָרִים is plural, and the clause is a simple nominal phrase ('graves are mine'). 'The grave is waiting for me' adds an idea not in the text; 'the graves are ready for me' stays closer while still reading naturally.

text: Surely mockers surround me, and my eyes must dwell on their hostility.
Give me, I pray, the pledge you require; who else will shake hands as my guarantor?

versions.text: Lay down a pledge for me with yourself. Who else will put up security for me?
versions.explanation: The particle נָּא ('please, I pray') is untranslated, and יִתָּקֵעַ לְיָדִי refers to the gesture of striking hands to seal a surety agreement, which the current rendering flattens.

text: You have closed their minds to understanding; therefore you will not let them triumph.
Whoever betrays his friends for a share of the spoil, the eyes of his children will fail.

versions.text: If a man denounces his friends for a price, the eyes of his children will fail.
versions.explanation: חֵלֶק means a 'share/portion' (of spoil or gain) rather than simply 'a price'; the proverbial force reads more smoothly as a relative clause than as a conditional.

text: He has made me a byword among the peoples, a man in whose face they spit.
My eyes have grown dim with grief, and all my limbs are but a shadow.
The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent are stirred up against the godless.
Yet the righteous holds to his way, and he whose hands are clean grows stronger.
But turn, all of you, and come again, I beg you! Yet I will find no wise man among you.

versions.text: But come back, all of you, try again! I will not find a wise man among you.
versions.explanation: 'Try again' is an interpretive addition not in the Hebrew (בֹאוּ נָא = 'come, please'), and the adversative force of the final clause ('yet... none') is clearer with 'no wise man'.

text: My days are past, my plans are shattered, and so are the desires of my heart.
These men turn night into day; in the face of darkness they say, 'Light is near.'
If the only home I hope for is the grave, if I spread out my bed in darkness,
if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother' or 'My sister,'
where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?
Will it go down with me to the bars of the grave? Shall we rest together in the dust?

versions.text: Will it go down to the gates of the grave? Shall we descend together into the dust?
versions.explanation: בַּדֵּי is better understood as the 'bars' of the underworld, and נָחַת carries the sense of settling or resting rather than only descending; the plural verb also refers to hope going down with the speaker.
